subject: English
source: Phase F · FEAT-PF1 — author-original scaffold rows for the highest-volume AQA Y10 English Language spec points (8700). Sentence frames support the AO2 language analysis question, the AO3 cross-text comparison, and the AO5/AO6 writing tasks.

sentenceFrames: The writer uses the [language feature: e.g. metaphor / verb / adjective] '______' which suggests ______.
This creates an effect of ______ for the reader, because ______.
The writer also uses [structural feature: e.g. short sentence / shift in time] which emphasises ______.

wordBank.definition: a comparison saying one thing is another (e.g. 'the city was a furnace')
giving human qualities to a non-human thing
the feelings or ideas a word brings to mind beyond its literal meaning
language that creates a picture in the reader's mind

stepLadder: Quote the writer's specific word, phrase or feature.
Name the technique (e.g. metaphor, verb choice, sentence form).
Explain what the technique suggests or implies.
Identify the effect on the reader and why.
Move to a second piece of evidence and repeat (build a paragraph of analysis).
commonPitfalls: Spotting techniques without explaining their effect.
Naming a technique that isn't actually present.
Quoting whole sentences when a single word or phrase would be sharper.
rows.visualAidHint: PEEZ paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explain, Zoom-in) keeps every paragraph tight.

sentenceFrames: Both writers express the view that ______. Source A makes this clear when ______; similarly, Source B uses ______ to ______.
However, Source A's tone is more ______, whereas Source B is more ______.

wordBank.definition: the writer's particular way of looking at the topic
the attitude conveyed by the writer's choice of words
the level of formality of the language used
combine ideas from two or more sources into a single point

stepLadder: Identify a clear point of similarity between the writers' views.
Comment on the methods each writer uses to convey that view.
Identify a clear point of difference.
Quote evidence from each source for the difference.
Comment on why the difference might exist (context / audience / purpose).
commonPitfalls: Discussing each source separately without comparing.
Using vague evaluative words (e.g. 'good', 'nice') instead of specific tone words.
